rows.reason: Within-span distractor's execution says it 'takes a true detail from the SAME sentence, line 2' — but 'John went with his master' is the previous sentence, and the option ('John came with him instead of the master') contradicts line 2 rather than reusing a true detail. Key (lines 2-3), hint and walk are correct.

Key 'strong and solidly built' correct from lines 6-9. But the 'Painted so they could be seen' distractor's execution ('reuses the idea of good rails as a warning') names an idea the passage never has, and the option copies no passage words, so en-inference-literal-lookalike does not name its mistake.

Tag en-relation-word-flipped (child hint: 'Some words tell you how two things go together') does not name this mistake: 'falling' reverses 'rising' (line 10), an antonym reversal with no relation word involved. Key, other distractors, hint and walk correct.

Minor: the fish-bait distractor's execution reads 'which this sentence does not fix' (should say the sense does not fit). Key 'a feed and a rest' is defensible for line 14; other distractors, hint and walk are sound.
Key (oak torn up by the roots, lines 22-24) is the only answer; branch/bridge/leaves distractors each excluded by line 20/47/4 as their executions say; hint and walk accurate.

Key matches 'I was not brought up to that' (line 26) with fear stated at 24-25; negation-dropped, plausible-not-stated and chronology (John reaches his head at 26-27) all hold; hint and walk accurate.

Tag en-relation-word-flipped (child hint: 'Some words tell you how two things go together') does not name this mistake: 'Drive slowly over the tree' drops the negative in 'we can't drive over that tree' (line 29), which is en-negation-dropped. Key (back to the crossways, six miles) correct; hint and walk accurate.

Key follows 'as that happened sometimes when the floods were out' (lines 33-34); dark (33 'could just see'), gatekeeper (43, to stop them) and good-pace (36 dead stop) distractors all excluded; hint and walk accurate.

Tag en-relation-word-flipped (child hint: 'Some words tell you how two things go together') does not name this mistake: 'The master knew that Beauty was right' contradicts his whip at lines 37-38; no relation word is flipped. Key (punished the thing that saved them, 37-38 vs 62-63) correct; hint and walk accurate.

Tag en-relation-word-flipped (child hint: 'Some words tell you how two things go together') does not name this mistake: 'the storm was still getting worse' ignores the lull at line 51, it does not flip a relation word. Key (slow, steady change) correct; quote on line 52 correct; hint and walk accurate.

Tag en-relation-word-flipped (child hint: 'Some words tell you how two things go together') does not name this mistake: 'Beauty had been badly trained' is an invented opposite judgement, not a flipped relation word. Key (would probably all have drowned, 55-58) correct; hint and walk accurate.
passageRef missing (row has passageRefMissing: true; it cannot show its passage). Also: stem gives no line references.
passageRef missing (row has passageRefMissing: true). Also: every distractor's execution is null, so criterion 3 cannot be checked.

Key follows line 1-2 ('began to think of the fun he had planned... and his sorrows multiplied'); jeering is future ('would come', line 2-3) so chronology distractor holds; others not stated; hint and walk accurate.

Key 'same sort of trash, but he paid nothing for it' misses the change the passage states (from not half enough to buy half an hour, line 6, to 'literally rolling in wealth', line 61), and 'paid nothing' is contestable — he traded turns at the fence for each item. Walk also misquotes line 60-61 as 'the middle of the day' (text: 'middle of the afternoon').

Key: the hop-skip-and-jump gait is what line 12 calls 'proof enough'; 'heart light and hopes high' is the mood proved, not the sign; calm (Tom, line 10) and apple distractors excluded; hint and walk accurate.

Key (the apple, line 19) correct and distractors excluded, but hintCore 'A small no sits in one line. Read it twice.' points to line 15's 'paid no attention' — the steamboat distractor's line — not to line 19, which carries no negative ('but he stuck to his work'). The hint steers the child to the wrong line.

Key (to make Ben doubt it is work) correct, but the 'answer the question Ben asked about work' distractor's execution says Ben's question only comes after (line 27). Ben has already asked about work at line 20 ('you got to work, hey?') and lines 23-24, so the execution is false and the distractor is partly supported by the window's run-up.

Key (make the job sound like a rare treat) correct; distractors excluded. walkScript says 'Rare is the word doing the work', but 'rare' is not in the passage — line 33 says 'every day'. Walk is not accurate to the text.
Key matches 'more and more interested, more and more absorbed' (36-37); daintily sweeping is Tom's (35), apple action is not a feeling, pity unstated; hint and walk accurate.

Second defensible answer: 'About one boy in a thousand could do it well' is close to what line 43 says (not one in a thousand, maybe two thousand) and it is itself a reason Tom gives for keeping the brush. Its negation-dropped execution overstates the difference. hintCore ('One of these drops a word that means no') also points at that distractor rather than helping to the key.

Key (each refusal raises the price, lines 49-52) supported; chronology (brush given at 53), motive and literal-lookalike distractors hold; hint and walk accurate ('back away' read as backing off consent at line 51).
Key 'keen and willing' fixed by the but-contrast with 'reluctance in his face' (line 53); relation-word-flipped correctly names reading but as and; hint and walk accurate.
Key 'want a thing badly' fits line 72-73; cover form-lookalike, jealous-of-person neighbouring sense and method distractors correctly excluded and tagged; hint and walk accurate.

hintCore 'Two of these are about the ending. Read the middle.' is false: only the three-coats option is about the ending. Also the chronology distractor's execution says 'line 53 has Ben give in' — line 53 is Tom giving up the brush; Ben gives in at line 52. Key itself is defensible.
Key (whether the thief has anywhere to go, lines 1-6) correct; shrewd-fellow is Stuart's aside, world-smaller is outside the window (10-11), England not named; hint and walk accurate.

Key defensible (remark, then instruction about the game, lines 7-8 and 81-82), but hintCore 'One of these joins his two speeches with an and' fits both the key ('and then tells them') and the literal-lookalike ('and then asks'), so it does not discriminate; walk's 'At line 81 he has staked half his fortune' cites line 74's fact at line 81.
Key 'set of games played through' fits 'the discussion fell during the rubber' (line 9); ball and eraser senses and the pause distractor excluded; hint and walk accurate.
Key (go round ten times more quickly, line 12) is Ralph's reason; result (line 13) and Stuart's rejoinder (line 14) correctly excluded; hint and walk accurate.
Key (three months vs eighty days, lines 18-19) correct and unique; weather is lines 21-22, outside the window; hint and walk accurate.

Key (he has allowed for every delay) correct, but 'He agrees those things were left out' is tagged en-negation-dropped while line 23 ('All included') contains no negative to drop — the option ACCEPTS Stuart's negative ('doesn't take into account', line 21). Tag does not name the mistake.

walkScript never reaches the meaning: after line 24 it moves to line 27 (the challenge) and line 31 ('quite possible'), neither of which bears on 'deal'. Also the stem asks the meaning of the phrase 'turn it was to deal' while options define 'deal'; window 'lines 24 to 31' is wider than the evidence.

Key (decided to wager after all, line 42) correct; but the wrong-scope distractor's execution states 'In the window, line 39 answers the stem: Come, let's go on with the game' — line 39 is the opposite of the answer; line 42 answers it.

Key (twenty thousand at Baring's, 45-46) correct; four thousand is Stuart's (42), minimum time is the objection (50-51), 'everything' overstated against 'half of his fortune' (74); hint and walk accurate.

Stem (and walk) say Sullivan says he is joking, but line 56 'You are joking.' is unattributed — the passage names Sullivan only at line 47. Not checkable from the text. Key is also only one of several things Fogg adds (57-58 'A true Englishman doesn't joke', the bet against anyone).

Key (uneasy feelings about rightness, lines 76-78) correct, but 'Careful scraping away at a surface' is tagged en-figurative-taken-literally while its execution says it is 'built from the scrape the word sounds like' — a form-lookalike mistake; nothing figurative is read literally.

Second defensible answer: 'The wager grows larger, and the card game goes on beside it' is true of the passage (29-46, with cards at 7, 15, 23, 40, 81), and the stem 'What happens every time the argument gets bigger?' does not ask for the relation the key adds. Distinction rests on the technique the stem never names.

Key (spring-cleaning, line 1) correct. walkScript says 'The other choices happen later in the passage' — false: aching back is line 4 (inside the window), and singing / painting the house blue and white never happen. Also 'Singing along with the happy birds' is tagged en-wrong-scope-retrieval while its execution says nothing states it (plausible-not-stated).
Key (splashes of whitewash, lines 3-4) correct and unique; dust (throat and eyes), straw (unstated), grass (line 15) and boat colours (line 60) excluded; hint and walk accurate.

Key (spring pulling at him, lines 5-9 'something up above was calling him imperiously') correct; aching back is the physical state not the trigger, Rat appears at 52-54, river motive unsupported; hint and walk accurate.
Key (the singing of the birds, line 18) correct; Christmas sense, bell, river (36) and shout (literal reading of 'almost like a shout', 19) distractors excluded; hint and walk accurate.

walkScript reasons 'contemptuous means looking down on someone. So he will not stop for anyone' — a non sequitur; the key (too excited to stop) rests on 'impatient' (line 23) and lines 19-20's joy, not on contempt. hintCore 'He is not thinking about the rabbits at all' is also contestable: he chaffs and jeers at them (24-26).
